description: Data engineers turning complex info into real-world solutions.
summary:
We developed Acauã (a bird of prey that carries strong symbolism in Brazilian folklore and popular culture), an agricultural decision-support platform built for smallholder family farmers and rural extension technicians in Brazil’s Semiarid region for the Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data challenge.

To address shifting rainy seasons, Acauã integrates daily NASA POWER precipitation and temperature data, NASA GIBS satellite layers (IMERG, SMAP L4, MODIS, SRTM), ISRIC SoilGrids, and Brazil’s official ZARC planting windows into a local Parquet/DuckDB lakehouse. A vectorized 10,000-scenario Monte Carlo simulator - paired with Markov soil-health modeling and FAO-56 crop water balance across 24 rainfed and irrigated crops—assesses whether conditions are safe to plant today and ranks multi-year crop rotations across a farm’s plots by food, forage, stability, or income.

This solution matters because delayed rainfall onset and mid-season dry spells (veranicos) frequently cause consecutive crop failures, threatening family nutrition and livestock survival. Acauã bridges satellite data and field reality by expressing probabilities in plain terms ("X out of 10 years"), delivered through a multi-page web app, printable technical PDFs, audio forecasts (O Rádio do Tempo), and an interactive text/voice assistant on web.
details:
Acauã (Motor Estocástico de Resiliência do Sertão) is a decision-support platform designed to help smallholder family farmers and rural extension technicians (EMATER and cooperatives) in Brazil’s Semiarid Northeast answer two critical seasonal questions: "Can I plant now?" and "Which crop rotation plan is most stable?" Rather than making decisions on behalf of farmers, the system synthesizes satellite earth observations, official government zoning, and stochastic simulation to support field-level planning with full transparency about data origins.

To evaluate whether conditions are safe to plant today, Acauã ingests daily corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) and minimum/maximum temperature (T2M_MIN, T2M_MAX) from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and GEOS-IT reanalysis, from 1981 onward) and detects confirmed rainy-season onset using the agronomic Sivakumar (1988) criterion - at least 20 mm accumulated within 3 days without a dry spell exceeding 7 days over the following 30 days. Comparing the ongoing season against the local 1991–2020 hydrological-year climatological median quantifies planting delay and dry-spell (veranico) climatology. In parallel, the platform queries Brazil’s official ZARC (MAPA/Embrapa, 2026/2027) risk tables filtered by municipal IBGE code, local soil textural group, and cultivar cycle across a two-year horizon, while an FAO-56 / Hargreaves evapotranspiration water-balance model computes root-zone dry-spell tolerance for rainfed crops and irrigation schedules ("Só com rega", including maximum interval and liters per m²) across 24 crops spanning 6 agronomic groups (9 rainfed grains, roots, and forages; 15 irrigated vegetables and fruits).

To evaluate multi-year farm resilience, Acauã runs a vectorized NumPy 10,000-scenario Monte Carlo engine with AR(1) climate persistence, calibrated with point-level NASA POWER seasonal rainfall statistics and paired with a discrete Markov soil-health chain modeling organic matter, available nitrogen, and fertilizer savings. A candidate generator builds valid combinations of 1 to 3 rainfed crops matching farmer constraints ("must include" and "must exclude"), ranking them against the property’s current planting baseline across 1, 2, 3, 5, or 10-year horizons according to five balance priorities: equilibrium, grain food production, herd forage, harvest stability (avoiding two consecutive failed seasons), and estimated income. When farmers register their farm area and individual plots (talhões) - optionally overriding ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 (250 m) and AWS SRTM terrain maps with field soil lab measurements - the planner distributes perennials and rotates annuals plot-by-plot across seasons, exporting month-by-month calendars in CSV and single-page A4 technical PDFs.

Beyond desktop dashboards, the platform is engineered for low-barrier accessibility and real-world rural connectivity. Its four-page Streamlit interface (Início, Plantio, Satélite, Conversa) includes interactive Folium maps layered with five NASA GIBS Earth observation lenses (IMERG precipitation, SMAP L4 soil moisture, MODIS NDVI vegetation vigor, MODIS land surface temperature, and SRTM elevation) resolved via OpenStreetMap Nominatim and IBGE boundaries, alongside “O Rádio do Tempo”, a regionalized audio briefing engine. On the Conversa tab, users can ask questions by text, voice note, or GPS pin; probabilities are translated from raw percentages into plain-language frequencies ("X out of 10 years/scenarios"), and active UI filters ("Resumo dos filtros escolhidos") are synchronized directly into session state.

From a software engineering standpoint, Acauã is built in Python (>= 3.11) around a local Medallion Lakehouse (data/bronze, data/silver, data/gold) using partitioned Parquet, DuckDB, Polars, Pandas, PyArrow, Pydantic, and HTTPX, with agronomic thresholds externalized in YAML configuration files (config/*.yaml), Plotly visualizations, Uvicorn/Starlette endpoints, gTTS, and optional OpenAI integration (gpt-5-nano function calling, gpt-4o-mini-transcribe speech-to-text, and gpt-4o-mini-tts), validated by 225 automated pytest tests (87% coverage) and Ruff linting. 

Crucially, the conversational AI layer incorporates strict anti-hallucination guardrails (guardas.py) ensuring all quantitative claims originate from deterministic tool calls rather than language-model estimation, and automatically degrades to a deterministic offline rule engine (regras.py) when AI services are unavailable. 

In designing the system, our team prioritized both regional agronomic validity and operational honesty. Because standard cumulative-anomaly onset methods can drift by more than 100 days during severe Semiarid droughts, we adopted Sivakumar (1988) and explicitly retained years in which rain never settled within the 1991–2020 baseline so climatic risk is never underestimated. We also enforced clear separation between real observed/official sources and model-reference assumptions (such as fixed baseline prices/costs, ~50 km NASA POWER pixel resolution, and missing phosphorus/potassium values without lab tests), and cached Bronze/Silver datasets locally so official ZARC zoning and offline advisory workflows remain functional under intermittent rural connectivity.
